yehud-medinata.t: Yehud Medinata, the small Persian province of Judah centred on Jerusalem's rebuilt temple, where Second Temple Judaism took shape.
yehud-medinata.o: After Cyrus of the Achaemenid Empire conquered Babylon in 539 BCE, Judaean exiles were allowed to return to Jerusalem. The province of Yehud was formed in the hills around the city, and under the governor Zerubbabel the Second Temple was completed c. 515 BCE.
yehud-medinata.r: Persian-appointed governors and the high priests of the temple shared authority. Nehemiah, a court official, rebuilt Jerusalem's walls c. 445 BCE, and Ezra brought the law of Moses to the centre of community life. The province minted small silver coins inscribed Yehud and used Aramaic for administration.
yehud-medinata.e: Yehud passed peacefully to Alexander of the Macedonian Empire in 332 BCE and then to the Ptolemaic Empire and the Seleucid Empire. The texts and institutions shaped there formed the basis of later Judaism.

yabghus-of-tokharistan.t: A Turkic dynasty that ruled Tokharistan, the old Bactria, from Kunduz, holding together a patchwork of principalities between the Turks, Tang China and the Arabs.
yabghus-of-tokharistan.o: After the Western Turkic Khaganate took Bactria from the Hephthalites, Tong Yabghu Khagan installed his son Tardu Shad as yabghu, or viceroy, of Tokharistan around 625, with his seat at Kunduz. Xuanzang met Tardu Shad there in 630 shortly before he was poisoned.
yabghus-of-tokharistan.r: The yabghus were overlords of some 27 local principalities, including Khuttal, Chaghaniyan and Bamiyan, many ruled by Hephthalite dynasties. Buddhism flourished, with great monasteries at Balkh and Bamiyan. Under Tang China's protectorate system the yabghus received Chinese titles and sent embassies asking for help against the Arabs, who took Balkh and pressed into the region from the 650s.
yabghus-of-tokharistan.e: The yabghus became vassals of the Umayyads, and the yabghu Nizak led a revolt crushed by Qutayba ibn Muslim in 710. The dynasty survived as Abbasid clients, with records of envoys to China until about 758, after which Tokharistan was absorbed into Islamic Khurasan.

yemen-arab-republic.t: North Yemen's republic, born in the 1962 revolution against the imamate, which fought a long civil war before uniting with the South in 1990.
yemen-arab-republic.o: On 26 September 1962 army officers led by Abdullah al-Sallal overthrew Imam Muhammad al-Badr of the Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen and proclaimed the Yemen Arab Republic. Egypt sent tens of thousands of troops to defend it, while Saudi Arabia backed the royalists.
yemen-arab-republic.r: The civil war lasted until 1970, when Saudi Arabia recognised the republic. Politics remained dominated by army officers and tribal leaders of the Hashid and Bakil confederations. President Ibrahim al-Hamdi was assassinated in 1977, and his successor too, before Ali Abdullah Saleh took power in 1978. Remittances from workers in Saudi Arabia sustained the economy, and oil was found near Marib in 1984.
yemen-arab-republic.e: After border wars in 1972 and 1979 and years of talks, North Yemen united with South Yemen on 22 May 1990 to form the Republic of Yemen, with Saleh as president.

yarkent-khanate.t: A Chagatai khanate of the western Tarim Basin, ruled from Yarkand, whose khans patronised poetry and Sufi orders until the Dzungars conquered it.
yarkent-khanate.o: In 1514 Sultan Said Khan, a descendant of Yunus Khan of Moghulistan, took Kashgar and Yarkand from the Dughlat amir Mirza Aba Bakr, founding a khanate with Yarkand as its capital. His cousin Mirza Muhammad Haidar Dughlat, author of the Tarikh-i Rashidi, served at his court.
yarkent-khanate.r: The khans ruled the oasis towns of Kashgar, Yarkand, Khotan and Aksu, with an agricultural economy and caravan trade to India and China. Under Abd al-Rashid Khan the court was a centre of music, and his queen Amannisa Khan is credited with compiling the Uyghur Muqam. In the 17th century the Naqshbandi Khoja families, divided into Aqtaghliq and Qarataghliq factions, became increasingly powerful.
yarkent-khanate.e: In 1680 the Aqtaghliq leader Afaq Khoja invited the Dzungar Khanate under Galdan Boshugtu, which conquered the khanate. The Khojas ruled as Dzungar vassals until the Chagatai line was formally ended around 1705.

yelang.t: The largest kingdom of the south-western peoples in Guizhou, remembered for a king who asked a Han envoy whether Han was larger than Yelang.
yelang.o: Yelang was a polity of the south-western peoples in western Guizhou and neighbouring Yunnan and Guangxi, emerging in the late Warring States period. It controlled the Zangke River route down to the Pearl River and the lands of Nanyue.
yelang.r: The Records of the Grand Historian describe Yelang as a settled kingdom of farmers with walled towns. Han envoys reached it in 135 BCE seeking a route to Nanyue, and the marquis Duotong accepted Han titles. Its ruler's question to the envoys about which state was larger gave rise to the Chinese idiom for self-importance born of ignorance.
yelang.e: After the Han Dynasty conquered Nanyue in 111 BCE, Yelang submitted and its ruler received the title of king, while Han established Zangke Commandery. Around 27 BCE the Han governor Chen Li executed the king, Xing, for rebellion and the kingdom was abolished.

yemen-vilayet.t: The second Ottoman province of Yemen, held against constant Zaydi revolts until the empire's defeat in 1918.
yemen-vilayet.o: The Ottoman Empire returned to Yemen in 1849, occupying the coastal Tihama and Hodeidah. After the opening of the Suez Canal increased the Red Sea's value, Ahmed Muhtar Pasha led an expedition that took Sanaa in 1872, ending the Qasimid State's last remnant and creating the Yemen Vilayet.
yemen-vilayet.r: The Ottomans introduced telegraphs, schools and courts and drew a border with the British Aden Protectorate in 1904-1914. Taxation and Sunni law provoked repeated Zaydi risings: Imam al-Mansur Muhammad and from 1904 his son Imam Yahya besieged Sanaa, and Ottoman losses were heavy. The Treaty of Da'an in 1911 gave Yahya authority over the Zaydi highlands under Ottoman sovereignty.
yemen-vilayet.e: Yahya stayed loyal during the First World War. After the armistice of 1918 the Ottoman garrisons withdrew and he took Sanaa, founding the Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen; the coast and the Idrisid Emirate of Asir followed different paths.

yan-five-dynasties.t: A brief empire proclaimed at Youzhou, near modern Beijing, by the warlord Liu Shouguang, crushed within two years by Jin.
yan-five-dynasties.o: Liu Rengong was military governor of Lulong, centred on Youzhou, in the late Tang. In 907 his son Liu Shouguang imprisoned him and seized the province. In 911, after declining offers from the Later Liang, Liu Shouguang proclaimed himself emperor of Great Yan.
yan-five-dynasties.r: Sources portray Liu Shouguang as arrogant and cruel, ruling by fear and heavy taxation. The state held the north-eastern frontier, bordering the rising Khitan of the future Liao dynasty, but had little support among its officials or neighbours.
yan-five-dynasties.e: Li Cunxu of Jin (Five Dynasties) sent his general Zhou Dewei against Yan in 911. Youzhou fell in 913, and Liu Shouguang was captured and executed with his father at Taiyuan in 914. Yan's territory became part of Jin and later of the Later Tang.

yettishar.t: The Kashgarian state of Yaqub Beg, created during the Muslim revolts against the Qing and recognised by Britain, Russia and the Ottomans.
yettishar.o: During the uprising against Qing rule in Xinjiang from 1864, Kashgar's rebels invited the Khoja Buzurg Khan from Kokand, accompanied by his general Yaqub Beg. Yaqub Beg soon sidelined Buzurg Khan, conquered Kashgar, Yarkand and Khotan, and by 1870 controlled most of the Tarim Basin, including Turpan and Urumqi.
yettishar.r: Yettishar, 'seven cities', was ruled by Yaqub Beg as Atalik Ghazi, with an army trained along Ottoman lines and strict enforcement of Islamic law. He signed trade treaties with Russia in 1872 and Britain in 1874, and the Ottoman sultan recognised him as emir. Heavy taxation and harsh rule caused resentment.
yettishar.e: The Qing general Zuo Zongtang reconquered Xinjiang from 1876. Yaqub Beg died at Korla in 1877, and his state collapsed. In 1884 the region became the Qing province of Xinjiang.

yueban.t: A nomad kingdom north of Kucha formed by Northern Xiongnu who stayed in Central Asia after the Han broke their power.
yueban.o: After Han China defeated the Northern Xiongnu in the late 1st century CE, part of them fled west. According to the Book of Wei, those too weak to continue settled north of Qiuci (Kucha), between the Tian Shan and the Tarbagatai, forming a state called Yueban in the 2nd century.
yueban.r: Chinese records describe a population of perhaps 200,000 who were cleaner in their habits than other Xiongnu, washing and cutting their hair, and who sent envoys to the Northern Wei court in the 440s. Little else is known of its government or economy beyond its pastoral way of life.
yueban.e: Yueban was overrun by the Rouran Khaganate and the Tiele in the late 5th century, and its people were absorbed into neighbouring steppe groups.

yufirid-dynasty.t: A highland Yemeni dynasty of the Himyarite tribe of Hiwal that held Sanaa and Shibam for over a century under nominal Abbasid rule.
yufirid-dynasty.o: Yu'fir ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Hiwali, from a Himyarite family, seized the highland fortress of Shibam Kawkaban around 847 and soon controlled Sanaa, ousting Abbasid governors while still naming the caliph in Friday prayers.
yufirid-dynasty.r: The Yufirids ruled a tribal highland state from Shibam and Sanaa, a rival to the Ziyadid dynasty in the coastal Tihama. They faced the arrival of the Zaydi imam al-Hadi in the north in 897 and the Isma'ili missionaries Ali ibn al-Fadl and Ibn Hawshab, who briefly captured Sanaa. As'ad ibn Ibrahim recovered the city and dominated highland politics in the early 10th century.
yufirid-dynasty.e: After As'ad's death in 944 the dynasty weakened through family feuds and tribal revolts. By about 997 it had lost Sanaa, and the highlands were contested between Zaydi imams, local chiefs and later the Sulayhid dynasty.

yemen-eyalet.t: The first Ottoman province of Yemen, conquered to fight the Portuguese and lost a century later to the Zaydi imams.
yemen-eyalet.o: In 1538 an Ottoman Empire fleet under Hadim Suleiman Pasha, on its way to fight the Portuguese in India, seized Aden and then Zabid. The Ottomans pushed into the highlands, taking Sanaa in 1547 under Ozdemir Pasha, and organised Yemen as a province.
yemen-eyalet.r: Ottoman governors relied on garrisons and allied tribes and faced constant resistance from the Zaydi Imamate of Yemen. A great revolt under al-Mutahhar in 1567 almost expelled them, until Sinan Pasha reconquered the country in 1569-1570. The province guarded the Red Sea approach to Mecca, and the coffee trade through Mocha began to grow in this period.
yemen-eyalet.e: In 1597 al-Qasim ibn Muhammad began a new Zaydi revolt. His son al-Mu'ayyad Muhammad continued it, and the Ottomans left Sanaa and evacuated Yemen in 1636, giving way to the Qasimid State.

yaaruba-dynasty.t: The Omani imamate that expelled the Portuguese from Oman and East Africa and turned Oman into the main naval power of the western Indian Ocean.
yaaruba-dynasty.o: In 1624 Ibadi scholars at Rustaq elected Nasir ibn Murshid al-Ya'rubi as imam, ending the rule of the Nabhani dynasty. He united the interior tribes and attacked the Portuguese coastal forts. His successor Sultan ibn Saif captured Muscat in 1650, ending Portuguese Muscat.
yaaruba-dynasty.r: The Ya'aruba built a navy and carried the war to East Africa, taking Fort Jesus at Mombasa in 1698 under Saif ibn Sultan and gaining influence over Zanzibar, Pemba and Kilwa. Trade in slaves, ivory and dates enriched the state. The imams built forts and palaces, including the round tower of Nizwa and the palace at Jabrin, and extended falaj irrigation.
yaaruba-dynasty.e: From 1718 disputed successions caused a civil war between the Hinawi and Ghafiri tribal factions, and one claimant invited Persian forces under Nader Shah. Ahmad ibn Said of Sohar expelled the Persians and was elected imam around 1744, founding the Omani Empire of the Al Bu Said.

yan-206-bc.t: The kingdom of Zang Tu in the Beijing region, created in 206 BCE, which switched sides to Liu Bang and was ended when its king rebelled against the new Han emperor.
yan-206-bc.o: Zang Tu was a general of the revived state of Yan who followed Xiang Yu to Julu and into the Qin heartland. In 206 BCE Xiang Yu made him King of Yan, with his capital at Ji (Beijing), and moved the previous king, Han Guang, to Liaodong. Zang Tu killed Han Guang and took Liaodong as well.
yan-206-bc.r: Yan was a frontier kingdom facing the Xiongnu and the Donghu, distant from the main theatres of the Chu-Han war. In 204 BCE, after Han Xin conquered Zhao, Zang Tu submitted to Liu Bang on the advice of the strategist Li Zuoche, without a battle.
yan-206-bc.e: Soon after Liu Bang proclaimed himself emperor in 202 BCE, Zang Tu rebelled. Liu Bang led the campaign himself, captured him and made his childhood friend Lu Wan King of Yan.

yuezhi.t: Nomads of the Gansu corridor who, driven west by the Xiongnu, conquered Bactria and gave rise to the Kushan Empire.
yuezhi.o: Chinese sources describe the Yuezhi as a powerful pastoral people between Dunhuang and the Qilian Mountains in the 3rd century BCE, strong enough to hold the young Xiongnu leader Modu as a hostage. Around 176 BCE the Xiongnu defeated them, and their king was later killed and his skull made into a drinking cup.
yuezhi.r: The main body, the Greater Yuezhi, migrated west through the Ili valley, displacing the Saka, then were pushed on by the Wusun to the Amu Darya. When the Han envoy Zhang Qian visited about 128 BCE they ruled Bactria from north of the river, governing through five xihou or princely chiefdoms. Their identification with the Tocharian-speaking peoples is widely held but debated.
yuezhi.e: In the 1st century CE Kujula Kadphises, chief of the Guishuang (Kushan) branch, united the five chiefdoms and founded the Kushan Empire. The Lesser Yuezhi who stayed behind in the Qilian Mountains merged with the Qiang peoples.

yiqu.t: A powerful Rong kingdom of the Loess Plateau that fought Qin for centuries, until a Qin queen dowager lured its king to his death in 272 BCE.
yiqu.o: The Yiqu were a Rong people of eastern Gansu and north-western Shaanxi, around modern Qingyang. By the 5th century BCE they had built walled towns and formed a kingdom strong enough to defeat the State of Qin in battle.
yiqu.r: The Yiqu combined farming with herding and controlled the uplands north of the Wei valley. Little is known of their institutions beyond Chinese accounts of wars and treaties with Qin. Excavated tombs of the region show a mixture of steppe-style ornaments and Chinese bronzes.
yiqu.e: According to the Records of the Grand Historian, Queen Dowager Xuan of Qin had a liaison with the king of Yiqu and bore him two sons, then had him killed at the Ganquan palace in 272 BCE. Qin annexed his lands, created the Longxi, Beidi and Shang commanderies and built a long wall to protect them.

ychsma.t: A coastal lordship of the Rímac and Lurín valleys centred on Pachacamac, the most famous oracle and pilgrimage site of the ancient Andes.
ychsma.o: Ychsma, or Ichma, emerged around 1100 in the Lurín and lower Rímac valleys, where modern Lima stands, after the decline of Wari influence. It took over Pachacamac, a sacred site occupied since the time of the Lima culture, and made it the heart of its territory.
ychsma.r: Ychsma was a group of lordships united around the cult of Pachacamac, the creator god whose oracle drew pilgrims from across the Andes. Its lords built a series of pyramids with ramps at Pachacamac and other sites such as Armatambo and Mateo Salado. The economy relied on irrigation canals drawn from the Rímac and on fishing.
ychsma.e: The Incas absorbed Ychsma peacefully around 1470 and respected Pachacamac, adding a Temple of the Sun and an Acllahuasi. In 1533 Hernando Pizarro looted the temple. Spanish Lima was founded in Ychsma territory in 1535, and Pachacamac is now a major archaeological site.

yamhad.t: Yamhad, the Amorite great kingdom of Aleppo, which dominated northern Syria in the 18th and 17th centuries BCE until the Hittites destroyed it.
yamhad.o: Sumu-epuh founded the kingdom at Halab, modern Aleppo, around 1810 BCE. He resisted Shamshi-Adad's Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia, and his son Yarim-Lim I made Yamhad the leading power of Syria, allied with Mari and Babylon; a Mari letter claims twenty kings followed him.
yamhad.r: Its great kings ruled through dependent kingdoms such as Alalakh in the Kingdom of Mukish and Ebla, and their prestige rested on the temple of the storm god Hadad on the Aleppo citadel. Wealth came from the trade between the Euphrates and the Mediterranean, and Hurrian culture spread widely among the elite.
yamhad.e: Hattusili I of the Hittite Empire attacked Yamhad, and Mursili I destroyed Aleppo c. 1595 BCE. A reduced kingdom survived until the Mitanni Empire absorbed it in the 16th century BCE. The Aleppo storm-god temple remained venerated for centuries.

yan-an-shi-rebellion.t: The rebel empire of An Lushan and Shi Siming, whose eight-year war nearly destroyed the Tang and left China's north-east in the hands of warlords.
yan-an-shi-rebellion.o: An Lushan, a general of Sogdian and Turkic descent and favourite of Emperor Xuanzong, commanded three frontier armies in the north-east. Fearing the chief minister Yang Guozhong, he rebelled at the end of 755, took Luoyang and early in 756 proclaimed himself emperor of Great Yan, capturing Chang'an that summer.
yan-an-shi-rebellion.r: The state was a military regime of frontier soldiers, including many Sogdian, Turkic and Khitan troops. It never governed securely: An Lushan was murdered by his son An Qingxu in 757, and Tang forces, aided by Uyghur cavalry, retook both capitals that year. Shi Siming killed An Qingxu in 759, retook Luoyang and was in turn murdered by his son Shi Chaoyi in 761.
yan-an-shi-rebellion.e: Shi Chaoyi was defeated and killed himself in 763 as his generals surrendered. Millions had died or been displaced, and the Tang Dynasty survived only by leaving the Hebei provinces to hereditary military governors, while the Tibetan Empire seized the north-west.

yeke-kingdom.t: Msiri's trading kingdom in Katanga, a crossroads of copper, ivory and slave routes, ended by a Congo Free State expedition in 1891.
yeke-kingdom.o: Msiri, a Nyamwezi trader from western Tanzania, arrived in Katanga around 1856. By backing local factions against the Kingdom of Kazembe and the Luba Empire, he made himself ruler, with his Yeke followers as the core of a new state centred on Bunkeya.
yeke-kingdom.r: Msiri's kingdom, known as Garanganze, controlled copper mines and caravan routes to both the Atlantic and Indian Ocean coasts. Ovimbundu and Swahili traders brought guns and cloth in exchange for ivory, copper and slaves. Msiri ruled through relatives, chiefs and warbands; the missionary Frederick Arnot settled at Bunkeya in 1886.
yeke-kingdom.e: In December 1891 Msiri was shot by Captain Omer Bodson of the Stairs Expedition, sent by the Congo Free State. Katanga passed to the Free State, and his successor Mukanda-Bantu became a subordinate chief.

yenisei-kyrgyz-khaganate.t: A Turkic people of the upper Yenisei who destroyed the Uyghur Khaganate in 840 and briefly ruled the Mongolian steppe.
yenisei-kyrgyz-khaganate.o: The Kyrgyz of the Minusinsk basin on the upper Yenisei were known to Chinese sources for centuries, subject in turn to the Turkic khagans and the Uyghur Khaganate. After a long war, in 840 a Kyrgyz army allied with a dissident Uyghur general sacked Ordu-Baliq, scattering the Uyghurs.
yenisei-kyrgyz-khaganate.r: The Kyrgyz ruler, titled ajo or khagan, ruled from the Yenisei and the Mongolian steppe, sending embassies to the Tang court. The Kyrgyz combined herding, farming and iron working, and left many stelae in the Old Turkic runic script along the Yenisei. Chinese sources describe them as tall, with red hair and green eyes.
yenisei-kyrgyz-khaganate.e: The Kyrgyz never fully moved their centre to Mongolia. In 924 the Khitan Liao dynasty drove them out of the Orkhon region, and they withdrew to the Yenisei. Their descendants are linked to the modern Kyrgyz and Khakas.

yaka-kingdom.t: A Lunda-founded kingdom on the Kwango river, ruled by the Kiamfu, which dominated the Yaka until Belgian conquest in 1906.
yaka-kingdom.o: In the 18th century Lunda warriors from the east, moving out from the Lunda Empire, conquered the Yaka and other peoples of the middle Kwango valley. Their leader took the title Kiamfu and founded a kingdom centred at Kasongo Lunda.
yaka-kingdom.r: The Kiamfu ruled through regional chiefs, many of Lunda descent, who paid tribute in slaves, ivory and raffia cloth. The kingdom acted as a middleman between the interior and Portuguese-linked traders in Kasanje and the Kongo region. Yaka initiation rites and masks became widely known in African art.
yaka-kingdom.e: The Congo Free State's forces fought the Kiamfu repeatedly in the 1890s and established control by 1906. The Kiamfu title survives as a customary office in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
